title: Constellations and nakshatras: the star patterns people see from Earth

summary.text: The seven stars of the Saptarishi look like a ladle, but they are not close together in space. Five of them are about 80 light-years away. The other two are much further. A constellation is a pattern of stars that people have named, and it has its shape only when seen from near Earth. People in every culture joined the stars into pictures and told stories about them. In India, astronomers split the Moon's path across the sky into 27 parts, the nakshatras. The Moon moves into about one new nakshatra each day. Stars also move very slowly, so in tens of thousands of years the constellations will change shape.
summary.art: A child on a city terrace at night pointing at the seven stars of the Saptarishi. Beside it, the same seven stars drawn from the side, five in a group and two far behind, joined by dotted lines back to the Earth.

intro.hook: Look at a picture of the Saptarishi, the seven bright stars that make a ladle in the northern sky. They look like seven lamps hanging side by side. Are they really side by side, or could some be much further away than others? How could we tell from down here?
intro.text: Every culture has looked at the night sky and joined the stars into pictures. In this unit you build a model of the Saptarishi with thread, using the real distances of its stars, and look at it from the side. You learn the nakshatras, the 27 star groups that the Moon passes through each month. You also find out how an astronomer showed, about 300 years ago, that the stars are moving.
intro.art: Seven paper stars hanging on threads at different distances in a dark room, with a child's eye at one end looking along the threads.

outcomes: I can explain what a constellation is, and that its stars are usually at very different distances from us.
I can build a thread model of the Saptarishi and use it to show why its shape is seen only from near Earth.
I can explain what the nakshatras are, why there are 27 of them, and that the Moon moves into about one new nakshatra each day.
I can tell how people in different cultures, in India and elsewhere, made different pictures and stories from the same stars.
I can explain that stars move, so constellations slowly change shape, and tell how Edmond Halley found this out.
I can get ready to look at stars from a city: let my eyes get used to the dark, use a red light, and say why city lights hide stars.

terms.meaning: A pattern of stars that people have named, such as the Saptarishi or Orion. Today astronomers divide the whole sky into 88 constellations, like a map divided into states.
terms.example: Orion is a constellation. The Greeks saw it as a hunter with a belt of three stars.
terms.art: The stars of Orion with faint lines joining them into a hunter with a belt of three stars.

terms.meaning: A well-known star pattern that is only part of a constellation, or made from stars of more than one.
terms.example: The Saptarishi is an asterism. Its seven stars belong to a bigger constellation called Ursa Major, the Great Bear.
terms.art: The seven stars of the Saptarishi drawn bright, inside the fainter outline of a big bear made of more stars.

terms.meaning: One of 27 star groups along the Moon's path across the sky. Indian astronomers named them to keep track of where the Moon is each night.
terms.example: Krittika is a nakshatra. It is a small, tight group of stars, called the Pleiades in English.
terms.art: A curved band across the night sky split into small parts, with a Moon in one of them and a tight little group of stars in the next.

terms.meaning: The distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 lakh crore kilometres. It measures distance, not time.
terms.example: Vasishtha, a star in the handle of the Saptarishi, is about 83 light-years away. The light you see from him tonight set off about 83 years ago.
terms.art: A beam of light leaving a star and a calendar beside it turning one year.

terms.meaning: A group of stars that really are close together in space. They were born together from the same cloud of gas and travel together.
terms.example: Krittika, the Pleiades, is a star cluster about 440 light-years away.
terms.art: A tight group of blue-white stars with a faint glow round them, seen close up.

terms.meaning: The way your eyes slowly get better at seeing in the dark. It takes about 20 to 30 minutes to see as many stars as you can.
terms.example: When you go from a bright room to a dark terrace, you see only a few stars at first. After 20 minutes you see many more.
terms.art: Two pictures of the same terrace sky: one with three stars, labelled 'after 1 minute', and one with thirty, labelled 'after 20 minutes'.

terms.meaning: Light from streetlights, buildings and signs that shines up into the sky and hides the fainter stars.
terms.example: From a big city you may see fewer than a hundred stars. Far from any town, on a clear dark night, you can see a few thousand.
terms.art: The same sky above a glowing city and above a dark village, with many more stars over the village.

explanations.concept: Constellations are patterns seen from Earth
explanations.definition: A constellation is a pattern of stars that people have named. Today it also means one of the 88 areas the sky is divided into, agreed by the International Astronomical Union in 1922.
explanations.description: The sky looks like a dark dome with stars stuck on it. But the stars are not on a dome. They are spread out through space at very different distances. A star pattern joins stars that happen to lie in the same direction from Earth. Some of them are near, and some are many times further away. The stars of the Saptarishi range from about 80 to about 123 light-years away. We see them as a ladle because we look from one place, near the Sun. From a planet round another star, the same stars would make a different pattern, or none at all.
examples: Kratu, the star at the top corner of the Saptarishi's bowl, is about 123 light-years away. Pulaha, just below him, is about 80 light-years away.

In Orion, Betelgeuse (the red star called Ardra or Thiruvathirai) is about 550 light-years away, while Bellatrix, on the other shoulder, is about 250. Astronomers are still refining the Betelgeuse distance.
Two fingertips, one near your eye and one at arm's length, can seem to touch. Move your head and they come apart. Stars in a constellation line up in the same way.
explanations.art: Seven stars seen from Earth as a ladle, and the same stars drawn from the side at their real distances, two far behind the other five.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the unit: why a constellation has its shape only from where we stand.

explanations.definition: The nakshatras are 27 equal parts of the Moon's path round the sky, each named after a star or a group of stars in it.
explanations.description: The Moon goes round the Earth. Against the stars, the Moon moves a little to the east each night. It comes back to the same stars after about 27 and one-third days. So Indian astronomers split the Moon's path into 27 parts, one for each day. The Moon passes into about one new nakshatra every day. The oldest lists, in the Vedas, begin with Krittika. Later lists begin with Ashwini. Chinese astronomers made a similar system of 28 'lunar mansions', and Arab astronomers had 28 'stations of the Moon'. Many South Indian families remember the nakshatra the Moon was in when a baby was born. Some celebrate birthdays on that star day.
examples: Onam is celebrated in Kerala on Thiruvonam, the day the Moon is in the nakshatra Shravana, in the month of Chingam.
Karthigai Deepam is lit in Tamil Nadu on the day the Moon is in Krittika, in the month of Karthigai.
Chitra is the bright star Spica. Swati is the bright orange star Arcturus. Rohini is the red star Aldebaran.
explanations.art: A circle of 27 small star groups round the sky, with the Moon drawn in one of them and arrows showing it moving to the next each night.
explanations.context: This card explains the nakshatras, the Indian way of tracking the Moon among the stars.

explanations.definition: Every star moves through space. From Earth, the nearer and faster stars shift slowly against the others, so constellations change shape over tens of thousands of years.
explanations.description: Stars look fixed because they are so far away. A car far down a long road seems to crawl, even when it is fast. In the same way, a star racing through space shifts by only a tiny amount in a human life. In 1718, Edmond Halley found that a few bright stars had moved since the time of Ptolemy, over 1,500 years before. Now we can measure every bright star's motion. Five stars of the Saptarishi travel together in the same direction. Kratu and Marichi, at the two ends, move differently. So in tens of thousands of years, the ladle will be bent out of shape.
examples: Arcturus, the nakshatra Swati, has moved about twice the width of the full Moon since Ptolemy's time.
Krittika's stars move together, so the cluster will keep its shape for a very long time.
explanations.art: The Saptarishi drawn three times: 50,000 years ago, today, and 50,000 years from now, with the two end stars drifting away from the other five.
explanations.context: This card explains why the patterns in the sky are not for ever.

explanations.definition: Your eyes see more stars after 20 to 30 minutes in the dark, and you see more stars where there is less light pollution.
explanations.description: Your eye has two kinds of light-sensing cells. One kind sees colour in bright light. The other kind works in dim light and slowly becomes much more sensitive in the dark. That is why more stars seem to appear the longer you wait. A white light, even a phone screen, undoes much of this in a moment. Red light disturbs it much less, which is why stargazers use red torches. City lights shining upwards light up the air, and the faint stars are lost in that glow. Bright stars and planets still shine through.
examples: During a power cut, many more stars appear above a city street after a few minutes.
In 2016, a team led by Fabio Falchi found that over 80 percent of the world's people live under light-polluted skies.
explanations.art: A child on a balcony with a phone torch covered in red cellophane, the city glowing orange below and a few bright stars above.
explanations.context: This card explains how to see as many stars as you can, even from a city flat.

explanations.concept: Why do so many cultures see seven sisters in Krittika?
explanations.description: Krittika, the Pleiades, is a small, tight group of stars. Most people can see six of them, sometimes seven. Stories from Greece, from many Aboriginal peoples of Australia and from North America speak of seven sisters, and often of one sister who is lost or hidden. In India, the Krittikas are six mothers who cared for the baby Kartikeya, called Murugan in Tamil Nadu. Nobody knows why such far-apart peoples tell such similar stories.
examples: In Greek stories, the Pleiades are seven sisters, and one of them is hard to see.
For the Maori of New Zealand, the rising of Matariki, the Pleiades, in midwinter marks the new year.

perspectives.who: Ray Norris and Barnaby Norris, astronomers (2021)
perspectives.explanation: The story may be over 100,000 years old, from before people spread out of Africa. Back then, two of the stars were further apart, so seven were easier to see. As they drew together, one sister 'disappeared'.

There is no need for one ancient story. In any culture, some people see six stars and some see seven. A story about a missing sister is a natural way to explain that, so it could have been invented many times.

explanations.art: The small group of Krittika stars with six bright and one faint, surrounded by small drawings of six mothers with a baby, seven sisters, and a Maori new-year scene.
explanations.context: This card is about a real puzzle: why do people far apart tell similar stories about the same few stars?

agreed.text: The stars of a constellation are usually at very different distances from us.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers measure star distances by parallax. As the Earth goes round the Sun, a near star seems to shift a little against the far ones. The Gaia spacecraft has measured the distances of over a billion stars this way.

agreed.text: Stars move through space, so constellations slowly change shape.
agreed.evidence: In 1718, Edmond Halley found that Sirius and Arcturus had moved since Ptolemy's star list of about 150 CE. Today their movements are measured every year.

agreed.text: The Moon comes back to the same stars about every 27 and one-third days.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see it. Note which star the Moon is near tonight. About 27 nights later it is back near the same star.

agreed.text: The sky is divided into 88 official constellations.
agreed.evidence: The International Astronomical Union agreed the list in 1922. The Belgian astronomer Eugene Delporte drew the borders between them, published in 1930.

agreed.text: Krittika, the Pleiades, is a real star cluster: its stars were born together.
agreed.evidence: Its stars are all about 440 light-years away and move together. They are about 100 million years old, young for stars.

agreed.text: City lights hide most stars from most people.
agreed.evidence: In 2016, Fabio Falchi and his team made a world map of sky brightness from satellite pictures and measurements on the ground. Over 80 percent of people live under light-polluted skies.

challenging.claim: The stars of a constellation are close neighbours, like a family living together.
challenging.who: Most people at first, and many children today
challenging.for: They look close together, and they move across the sky together every night.
challenging.against: Measured distances show they are usually far apart. Kratu in the Saptarishi is about 43 light-years further away than Pulaha, the star just below him. They move across the sky together only because the Earth spins.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea of what a constellation is.

challenging.claim: The stars are fixed, so the constellations keep their shapes for ever.
challenging.who: Most astronomers, from ancient Greece and India until about 300 years ago
challenging.for: In one lifetime, or even in a thousand years, nobody can see a constellation change by eye.
challenging.against: In 1718 Edmond Halley showed that bright stars had moved since Ptolemy's time. Today we measure every bright star's movement.
challenging.context: This card is about the old name 'the fixed stars', and why it was wrong.

challenging.claim: The nakshatra or star sign a person is born under shapes their character and their future.
challenging.who: Astrology, followed by many people in India and around the world
challenging.for: It is a very old tradition, and many people feel their star describes them well.
challenging.against: In 1985 the physicist Shawn Carlson ran a careful test. Astrologers tried to match people's birth charts to their personality tests. They did no better than guessing. Using a birth star to choose a name or to time a festival is part of culture. Whether the stars shape a person is a question that tests have answered no.
challenging.context: This card is about the difference between star names in our culture and the claim that stars decide our lives.

challenging.claim: The story of the seven sisters in Krittika is over 100,000 years old.
challenging.who: Ray Norris and Barnaby Norris, astronomers, in 2021
challenging.for: Peoples who had been apart for tens of thousands of years tell similar stories about the cluster and a lost sister. Long ago, one star was further from its neighbour, so it was easier to see.
challenging.against: A missing-sister story could be invented again and again, because some people see six stars and some see seven. There is no way to test a story that old directly.
challenging.context: This card is about a bold idea on how old our star stories might be.

big_questions.q: The Saptarishi is a ladle only from near Earth. Is the ladle real, or is it something we make by looking?
big_questions.hint: Think of the thread model. From the Earth card you saw a ladle. From the side you did not. Were the paper stars different?

big_questions.q: If you lived on a planet round Kratu, what patterns would you see? Would you see our Sun?
big_questions.hint: Our Sun is about 123 light-years from Kratu. From there, the Sun would be a faint star. Which other stars might look near it?

big_questions.q: Why did people all over the world, who never met, all join the stars into pictures and stories?
big_questions.hint: What did the stars help them do? Think of farmers, sailors and festivals.

big_questions.q: The Pleiades are called six mothers in India and seven sisters in Greece. Which story is right?
big_questions.hint: Can two stories about the same stars both be true in their own way? What would a scientist say is true about the stars?

big_questions.q: Light from Kratu left about 123 years ago. Are you seeing Kratu as he is now, or as he was?
big_questions.hint: Who in your family was alive 123 years ago? What could have changed since?

big_questions.q: In 50,000 years the ladle will be bent out of shape. Will anyone then still call it the Saptarishi?
big_questions.hint: Names stay when things change. Think of a town that kept its old name after it grew.

story.title: Arundhati Behind the Streetlights
text: On the night before her cousin Revathi's wedding, Lakshmi sat on the terrace of her grandmother's house in Kumbakonam. It was May, and the power had gone off, as it often did. The whole street was dark. Above the water tank, the sky was full of stars.

'Look north,' said Paati, her grandmother. She pointed past the coconut trees. 'Do you see seven bright stars, like a big ladle? That is the Saptarishi, the seven sages.' Lakshmi found four stars in a box and three stars in a curved handle. Paati named them one by one: Kratu, Pulaha, Pulastya, Atri, Angiras, Vasishtha and Marichi.

'Now look hard at Vasishtha, the middle star of the handle,' said Paati. 'Can you see a tiny star just beside him?' Lakshmi stared. At first she saw nothing. Then, as her eyes got used to the dark, a faint speck appeared, close to Vasishtha. 'That is Arundhati, his wife,' said Paati. 'At many weddings, the couple is shown Arundhati. The two stars are always together, and the couple should be too.'

The next day the wedding hall was loud with nadaswaram music and bright with tube lights. After the thali was tied, the priest spoke about Arundhati. Vikram, the groom, leaned over to Lakshmi and whispered, 'I have never actually seen this star. In Chennai I can hardly see any stars at all.' Lakshmi grinned. 'I can show you tonight,' she said.

That evening, when most of the guests had gone, Lakshmi took Vikram up to the terrace. This time the power was on. The streetlights glowed orange, and a shop sign flashed below. Lakshmi found the ladle easily, because its seven stars are bright. But when she looked for Arundhati, there was nothing beside Vasishtha. 'She is hidden,' said Lakshmi. 'The lights are too bright.'

Vikram took out his phone to look up a sky map. 'Don't,' said Lakshmi. 'Paati says your eyes need time in the dark. The phone screen undoes it.' Just then, the power went off again. Somebody downstairs groaned. Lakshmi laughed. 'Now wait,' she told Vikram. 'Don't look at anything bright for a while.'

They sat on the parapet and waited, talking softly. Slowly, more stars came out, as if someone were switching them on one by one. After about fifteen minutes Vikram said, 'There. Next to Vasishtha. A tiny one.' He sounded as pleased as if he had found a coin on the road. 'They really are side by side,' he said. 'Like two houses on one street. All seven stars are, I suppose.'

Lakshmi frowned. In her science book there was a page about the Saptarishi. It said that the stars of a star pattern are usually not close to each other at all. 'Not all of them,' she said. 'Kratu, at the top of the bowl, is much further away than the others. Marichi, at the end of the handle, is further too. The seven stars only make a ladle from here.'
'So the ladle is not real?' asked Vikram.

'It is real from here,' said Lakshmi. She held up one finger close to her eye and another at arm's length, and moved them until the fingertips seemed to touch. 'Look. From my eye they touch.' Vikram leaned to the side. From where he sat, the two fingertips were far apart, one near Lakshmi's nose and one out by the parapet. He laughed. 'All right, teacher,' he said. 'So is Arundhati a trick too? Is she really far behind Vasishtha?'

Lakshmi did not know. She thought about it all through dinner. The next morning, she asked her mother to help her look it up. They found that Vasishtha is about 83 light-years away. Arundhati is about 82 light-years away. The two stars are really close together in space, and they move through space together. Astronomers are still checking whether they slowly go round each other.

Lakshmi ran to find Vikram, who was packing the car with Revathi. 'Arundhati is not a trick,' she said, out of breath. 'Most of the ladle is a view from Earth. But Arundhati and Vasishtha really are neighbours. They travel together.'
Vikram put down a suitcase. 'So the old story picked the one pair in the ladle that really is a pair,' he said. 'Did the people who made it know that?'

'Nobody could have measured it then,' said Lakshmi. 'Maybe it was luck. Maybe they just loved them for always being together.' Revathi laughed and hugged her. 'When we are in Chennai,' Vikram promised, 'I will go up on our terrace during a power cut and look for them.' 'Then switch off your phone first,' said Lakshmi. 'And wait.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: from Earth, the seven stars of the Saptarishi look like a single group, but they are at different distances, so the ladle is a pattern seen from one place. Vikram assumes that stars which look together are together. Lakshmi knows they usually are not. Then comes a surprise: Arundhati (Alcor) and Vasishtha (Mizar) really are close in space and move together. So a pattern seen from Earth can hide real neighbours as well as false ones. Only measuring distances can tell which is which. The story also shows why the dark matters: with the streetlights on, Arundhati vanished.
ask: Why could Lakshmi see Arundhati on the first night but not when the streetlights were on?
Why did Lakshmi tell Vikram not to look at his phone?
Vikram thought all seven stars were side by side. How did Lakshmi show him that two things can look together but be far apart?
What did Lakshmi find out about Arundhati and Vasishtha that surprised her?
Lakshmi says the ladle is 'real from here'. What do you think she means?

story.note: Lakshmi, Paati, Revathi, Vikram and their family are made up. The Arundhati custom is real and is followed at many weddings in South India and elsewhere. Arundhati is the star Alcor and Vasishtha is Mizar. Their distances, about 82 and 83 light-years, are from star surveys. Alcor can be seen by eye on a dark night.

printables.title: A paper Moon token, and 20 small star tokens

rules: Put the Moon token on Ashwini. Shuffle the question cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take a card and read it out. Answer it using the board.
A right answer wins a star token. Then move the Moon token on by one space, because one more night has passed.
A SKY CARD can be done tonight. If you do it, you win two star tokens tomorrow.
When the Moon token has gone all the way round the ring, back to Ashwini, the game ends. The player with the most star tokens wins.
Count the turns at the end: the Moon took 27 turns to go round, just as the real Moon takes about 27 days.

flow.do: 1. Lay the board on the floor. 2. Put the Moon token on Ashwini. 3. Shuffle the cards.
flow.say: This ring is the Moon's path round the sky, split into 27 nakshatras. Each turn is one night. The Moon moves one space each night.
flow.kid: This ring is the Moon's path. It has 27 nakshatras. Each turn is one night. The Moon moves one space.

ask.q: What does the count tell us?
good: 27 turns, so the real Moon takes about 27 days to go round the stars.

experiments.title: The Thread Saptarishi: are its seven stars really close together?
experiments.question: Are the seven stars of the Saptarishi at the same distance from us? Does their ladle shape still show when you look from somewhere other than Earth?
experiments.predict: Before you build it, guess. When you look at the model from the side, will the seven stars still make a ladle? Will they all be the same distance from Earth? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Build the model once, using the real distances, and do not move the paper stars. Change only one thing: where you look from. Look with one eye closed each time, with your eye at the same height as the Earth card.
results_table: Did I see the ladle? (yes, a little, no)
Which paper stars looked closest together

materials.item: sewing thread or thin string, cut into 7 pieces each about 1 and a half metres long
a sheet of chart paper, or two sheets of newspaper taped together, about 50 cm across
a piece of cardboard from a box, about the size of a postcard (the Earth card)
a chair, cellotape and a sharp pencil
a measuring tape, or a 30 cm school ruler
7 small paper stars, about 2 cm across, cut from bright or white paper

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the card with the pencil, pushing into an eraser or folded cloth, never towards a hand. Keep the threads away from the doorway, so nobody trips on them.

schedule.what: Guess. Mark the seven stars on the wall. Stretch a thread from the Earth card to each star. Fix each paper star at its real distance. Look from the Earth card, then from the side, and record what you see.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table for each place you looked from. Draw the model twice: as seen from the Earth card, and as seen from the side.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the picture of the Saptarishi in the app. 2. Ask the guess question below and wait for the answer and the reason.
flow.say: These seven stars make a ladle. If we could fly out into space and look from the side, would they still look like a ladle? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the seven stars of the Saptarishi. They make a ladle. Would they still look like a ladle from the side? Guess. Say why.

ask.q: Do you think all seven stars are the same distance from us? Why?
good: Yes, because they look like they are in a row.
Maybe not. Far things look small, so the faint ones could be further.

flow.parent: Accept any guess with a reason. Do not say the answer. The model will show it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Thread Saptarishi experiment. You build a model of the seven stars at their real distances, then look at it from different places.

flow.do: 1. Tape the chart paper flat on a wall at your child's eye height when kneeling. 2. Measure from the bottom left corner of the paper and mark seven dots, using the list in the note. 3. Write each star's name next to its dot.
flow.say: This paper is the far sky. Let's mark where the seven stars are. Measure across from the left edge first, then up from the bottom.
flow.kid: This paper is the sky. Measure across, then up. Mark each star with a dot. Write its name.
flow.parent: Dot positions, in centimetres from the bottom left corner: Marichi 5 across and 5 up. Vasishtha 14 across and 13 up. Angiras 22 across and 14 up. Atri 31 across and 15 up. Pulastya 37 across and 10 up. Pulaha 49 across and 17 up. Kratu 46 across and 26 up. The dots make the ladle at the right size for the model.
flow.context: In this step of the Thread Saptarishi experiment, you mark the seven stars on paper on a wall.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pokes a hole in the middle of the Earth card with a sharp pencil. 2. Tape the card upright to the back of a chair, about 1 metre from the wall. 3. Make the hole level with the dots. 4. Tape one end of each thread to the front of the card, right at the edge of the hole.
flow.say: This card is the Earth. We will look at the stars through this hole. Every thread starts at the Earth.
flow.kid: The card is the Earth. A grown-up makes a hole in it. Tape all seven threads next to the hole.
flow.parent: The threads should start as close to the hole as you can get them, so they all seem to come out of your child's eye. If your room is small, 80 cm from the wall also works.

flow.do: 1. Stretch each thread from the card to one dot. 2. Pull it straight but not too tight, and tape it on the dot. 3. Measure along each thread from the card, and tape a paper star there. Use the distances in the note.
flow.say: Each centimetre along the thread stands for 2 light-years. Kratu is about 123 light-years away, so his paper star goes at about 62 centimetres.
flow.kid: Stretch each thread to its star dot. Tape it. Measure along the thread. Tape the paper star at the right place.
flow.parent: Distances along each thread from the card, at 1 centimetre for 2 light-years: Kratu (Dubhe) 62 cm, Pulaha (Merak) 40 cm, Pulastya (Phecda) 42 cm, Atri (Megrez) 40 cm, Angiras (Alioth) 41 cm, Vasishtha (Mizar) 41 cm, Marichi (Alkaid) 52 cm. The real distances are about 123, 80, 83, 81, 83, 83 and 104 light-years. Fold each paper star over its thread and tape it so it does not slide.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands behind the chair, closes one eye and looks through the hole in the Earth card. 2. They describe what they see and fill in the first row of the table.
flow.say: Look through the hole with one eye. What shape do the seven paper stars make?
flow.kid: Close one eye. Look through the hole. What shape do the paper stars make? Write it down.

ask.q: Do the paper stars make the ladle?
good: Yes, each paper star sits right on its dot.
It looks just like the picture.

flow.do: 1. Now your child walks to one side of the model, halfway between the card and the wall. 2. They look at the paper stars from the side. 3. They fill in the second row, and sketch what they see.
flow.say: Now you are on a planet out to the side. Look at the seven paper stars. Do they still make a ladle?
flow.kid: Walk to the side. Look at the paper stars. Is it still a ladle? Which stars are close together? Sketch it.

ask.q: Which paper stars are far from the others?
good: Kratu and Marichi are further back, near the wall.
Five are in a bunch, and two are far behind.

check.q: From the side, what did the seven paper stars look like?
options: Five close together, and two much further from Earth
check.why: Five stars are about 80 light-years away, so their paper stars sit about 40 centimetres along. Kratu is at 62 centimetres and Marichi at 52, much nearer the wall. If you saw a ladle from the side, check that you are halfway along, looking across the threads.

flow.do: Ask your child to find any other place in the room where the ladle shows. Try a step to the left of the chair, a step to the right, and standing on tiptoe.
flow.say: Can you find anywhere else in the room where the seven stars still make the ladle?
flow.kid: Hunt for another spot where you see the ladle. Try left, right, and on tiptoe.
flow.parent: Your child should find that the ladle shows only when the eye is at or very close to the Earth card. A step away and the shape bends.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why does it happen?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the seven stars of the Saptarishi are not all close together. What I saw: from the Earth card they made a ladle, but from the side five were in a group and two were far behind. Why: the stars only line up in that shape when you look from Earth. Now explain: a constellation is a pattern seen from one place. From a planet round another star, the same stars would make a different pattern.

experiments.title: Eyes in the Dark: how long do your eyes take to see faint stars?
experiments.question: How many faint 'stars' on a paper can you see in a dark room after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 10 minutes and 15 minutes?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will you see more stars, fewer, or the same number as the minutes go by? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same paper, in the same place, with the same tiny bit of light in the room every time. The same person counts each time. Change only one thing: how long you have been in the dark.
results_table: Number of stars I can see (out of 12)

materials.item: a sheet of white paper
a black sketch pen and an ordinary pencil
a room that can be made nearly dark at night, with a thin line of light under the door
a clock or timer that does not light up, or a grown-up outside the room calling out the time

experiments.safety: Clear the floor before switching off the light, so nobody trips. A grown-up stays close by.

schedule.what: Draw 12 stars, from very dark to very faint. Sit in the dark and count how many you can see after 1, 5, 10 and 15 minutes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each time.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up draws 12 small stars on the white paper, without your child watching. 2. Make 2 with the black sketch pen, 3 with the pencil pressed hard, 3 pressed medium, and 4 pressed very lightly. 3. Scatter them over the page.
flow.say: I'm drawing some stars on this paper. Some are dark and some are very faint, like real stars. Don't peek yet.
flow.kid: A grown-up draws 12 stars. Some are dark. Some are very faint. Don't peek!
flow.parent: Mixing the stars around the page stops your child from counting them by memory. The faintest ones should be just visible in normal room light.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Eyes in the Dark experiment. You find out how long your eyes take to get used to the dark, which is why stargazers wait before looking.

flow.do: 1. Prop the paper against a wall at the far side of the room, about 2 metres from where your child will sit. 2. Ask the guess question.
flow.say: When I switch off the light, you will count the stars you can see. Will you see more as time goes on, or fewer, or the same? Why?
flow.kid: Soon the light goes off. You will count the stars. Will you see more, fewer, or the same as time goes on? Why?

good: My eyes get used to the dark.
When I wake at night I can see more after a while.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the light. Leave only a thin line of light under the door. 2. After 1, 5, 10 and 15 minutes, your child counts the stars and calls out the number. 3. You write the numbers down without a bright light. A grown-up can call out the time from outside.
flow.say: Now count. How many stars can you see? We'll count again in a few minutes.
flow.kid: Count the stars you can see. Say the number. Wait. Count again when the grown-up says.
flow.parent: If your child cannot see any stars even after 15 minutes, open the door a little more. If they see all 12 at once, the room is too bright: close the curtains or the door more. While you wait, chat quietly or tell the Krittika story from this unit.

flow.do: Switch the light back on. Ask your child to say or write what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.

check.q: In the dark, you saw more stars the longer you waited. Why?
options: The stars on the paper got darker
My eyes slowly got better at seeing in dim light
The light under the door got brighter
check.why: Nothing on the paper changed, and the room stayed the same. Your eyes changed. Cells in your eye that see in dim light become much more sensitive after 20 to 30 minutes in the dark. This is called dark adaptation. If you picked 'the light under the door got brighter', check it next time: it stays the same.

flow.parent: A good answer: what I think, my eyes get better in the dark. What I saw, after 1 minute I saw 3 stars, and after 15 minutes I saw 10. Why, my eyes got used to the dark. Then explain: this is why stargazers wait 20 minutes on the terrace before they look for faint stars, and do not look at a phone.

experiments.title: The Moon's Daily Step: how far does the Moon move among the stars?
experiments.question: Against the stars, how far does the Moon move from one night to the next, and in which direction?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you look at the Moon at the same time tomorrow night, will it be in the same place among the stars, or somewhere else? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Look at the same time each night, from the same spot on the balcony or terrace. Measure with your fist held out at arm's length, the same way every time.
results_table: Fists from that star to the Moon
Moon east or west of the star
Nakshatra (from a sky app, if you have one)

materials.item: a balcony, window or terrace where you can see part of the evening sky
a notebook and a pencil
a free sky map, such as Stellarium Web, on a phone or computer, used by a grown-up with the screen dimmed (optional)

experiments.safety: A grown-up stays with the child on the balcony or terrace at night. Keep away from the edge of a terrace without a wall.

schedule.what: Find the Moon at 7:30 in the evening. Measure in fists from a bright star nearby. Note the time.
Same time, same spot. Measure again from the same star.
Same time, same spot. Measure again.
Look at your table. Work out how far the Moon moves each night, and how long it would take to go all the way round.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each night. Draw the star and the Moon each night on one page, so you can see the Moon stepping along.

flow.do: 1. Choose a week when the Moon is a crescent or half Moon in the evening sky. 2. That is about 3 to 8 days after Amavasya, the new Moon. 3. Ask the guess question.
flow.say: Tomorrow at the same time, will the Moon be in the same place among the stars, or somewhere else? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Will the Moon be in the same place among the stars tomorrow? Guess. Say why.

good: The Moon moves round the Earth.
The Moon looks different each night, so maybe it moves.

flow.parent: A calendar that shows Amavasya and Purnima helps you pick the week. In the week after Amavasya, the Moon is in the western sky in the early evening.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Moon's Daily Step experiment. Over a few nights you measure how far the Moon moves among the stars.

flow.do: 1. At 7:30 in the evening, find the Moon. 2. Find the brightest star near it. 3. Hold your fist out at arm's length and count how many fists fit between the star and the Moon. 4. Write it down, and whether the Moon is east or west of the star.
flow.say: Hold your fist out straight, like this. How many fists fit between that bright star and the Moon?
flow.kid: Hold your arm out straight. Make a fist. Count fists from the bright star to the Moon. Write it down.
flow.parent: A fist at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky, for children and grown-ups alike. If a building hides the star, choose another bright star and use it every night. If it is cloudy, skip that night and note the date.

flow.do: On the next two nights, at the same time and from the same spot, measure again from the same star.
flow.say: Same time, same star. Where is the Moon tonight? How many fists away?
flow.kid: Same time. Same star. Count the fists again. Did the Moon move?
flow.wait: Do this on the next two nights, at the same time.
flow.parent: The Moon should be about one and a third fists further east each night, away from where the Sun set. Because the Moon also rises about 50 minutes later each day, it will look higher in the sky each evening.

flow.do: On day 4, look at the table together. Ask your child to say what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: How far did the Moon move each night? If it keeps going, how many nights to go all the way round the sky?
flow.kid: How far did the Moon move each night? Which way? Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

check.q: The Moon moves about one nakshatra each night. There are 27 nakshatras. About how long does the Moon take to come back to the same stars?
check.why: One nakshatra a night, and 27 nakshatras, makes about 27 nights. The real time is about 27 and one-third days. That is why Indian astronomers made 27 nakshatras: one for each day of the Moon's trip round the sky.

flow.parent: A good answer: what I think, the Moon moves east among the stars every night. What I saw, on night 1 it was 1 fist from the star, on night 2 a little over 2 fists, on night 3 about 3 and a half. Why, the Moon is going round the Earth. Then explain the nakshatras: the Moon's path is split into 27 parts, so it enters about one new nakshatra every night.

activities.title: One Sky, Many Pictures: join the dots your own way

materials.item: the dot picture of the stars of Orion in the app, printed or copied onto paper without lines
a pencil and colour pencils

schedule.what: Join the dots into your own picture. Then see how the Greeks and Indian astronomers joined the same stars.

activities.record: Keep your drawing. Under it, write the name and the story of your picture.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the dot picture. Do not say what it is. 2. Ask them to join any of the dots into a picture of anything they like.
flow.say: These dots are real stars that you can see from our balcony in winter. Join some of them to make a picture. It can be anything at all.
flow.kid: These dots are real stars. Join some of them. Make a picture of anything you like.
flow.parent: There is no right answer. Children often draw a person, a kite, a butterfly or an animal.
flow.context: This is the first step of the One Sky, Many Pictures activity. You make your own star picture before learning other people's.

flow.do: Show the two old pictures in the app. One is the Greek hunter Orion. The other is the Indian Mrigashira, the deer's head, with the red star Ardra nearby.
flow.say: The Greeks saw a hunter with a belt of three stars. In India, astronomers saw the head of a deer, Mrigashira, and named the red star Ardra. In Tamil it is Thiruvathirai.
flow.kid: The Greeks saw a hunter here. Indian astronomers saw a deer's head. The red star is Ardra.

ask.q: Which picture do you like best, yours or theirs? Why?
good: Mine, because it looks like a kite.
The hunter, because the belt is easy to find.

flow.do: Ask the question below and let your child think.
flow.say: Three people joined the same stars and made three different pictures. Were the stars different?
flow.kid: Three people saw three different pictures. Were the stars different?

check.q: The Greeks saw a hunter and Indian astronomers saw a deer's head in the same stars. Why?
options: They were looking at different stars
People join the same stars into different pictures
The stars moved between Greece and India
check.why: The stars are the same. The pictures come from the people who joined them. Every culture made its own pictures. If you picked 'the stars moved', that is a good thought, because stars do move, but only very slowly. Both pictures are about 2,000 years old or more.

flow.think: If a child on another planet joined these dots, what might she see?

activities.title: Find the Saptarishi from Your Balcony

materials.item: a balcony, window or terrace that faces north, or a spot where you can see the northern sky
a red stargazing torch (from the Red Torch activity), or no torch
a free sky map such as Stellarium Web, used by a grown-up with the screen dimmed (optional)

activities.safety: A grown-up stays with the child at night. Keep away from the edge of a terrace without a wall.

schedule.what: On a clear evening, switch off the lights near you, wait 15 minutes, and look for the Saptarishi in the north. In the months when the Saptarishi is not up in the evening, look for Krittika or Orion instead.

activities.record: Draw the stars you found, and the buildings or trees below them, so you can find them again.

flow.do: Check the month. From about February to June, the Saptarishi is up in the north in the evening. From about November to March, Krittika and Orion are high in the evening sky.
flow.say: Tonight we hunt for a star pattern from home. First, let's find which way is north.
flow.kid: Tonight you hunt for a star pattern. First, find north. The Sun sets in the west. North is to its right.
flow.parent: If you are not sure which patterns are up, a free sky map like Stellarium Web shows tonight's sky for your town.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Find the Saptarishi activity. You look for real star patterns from home.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the lights in the room behind the balcony. 2. Wait about 15 minutes without looking at a phone. 3. Look for seven bright stars making a ladle, low in the north.
flow.say: Let's give our eyes time. While we wait, tell me what you remember about the thread model.
flow.kid: Switch off the lights. Wait 15 minutes. No phone! Then look north for seven stars like a ladle.
flow.parent: In much of South India the Saptarishi is quite low in the north, so tall buildings may hide part of it. Try different windows or the terrace. If you find the ladle on a dark night, look next to Vasishtha, the middle star of the handle, for tiny Arundhati.

flow.do: Ask your child what they found.
flow.say: Which stars did you find? Were they all equally bright?
flow.kid: Which stars did you find? Were they all equally bright?

ask.q: If a star looks faint, does that mean it is further away?
good: Not always. Some stars are just less bright.
Maybe, but Kratu is the furthest and he is still bright.

activities.title: Krittika Round the World: one star cluster, many stories

materials.item: paper and colour pencils

schedule.what: Hear four stories about the same small group of stars. Draw one of them, and make up your own.

activities.record: Draw the cluster in the middle of a page and your favourite story round it.

flow.do: Read out the four short stories in the note, one by one. Show the picture of Krittika after each.
flow.say: These four stories are all about the same small group of stars. Listen, and tell me what is the same in them.
flow.kid: Listen to four stories. They are all about the same few stars. What is the same in them?
flow.parent: 1. India: the six Krittikas are mothers who cared for the baby Kartikeya, called Murugan in Tamil Nadu. 2. Greece: the Pleiades are seven sisters, and one is hard to see. 3. Many Aboriginal peoples of Australia: seven sisters are chased across the sky by a man. 4. The Maori of New Zealand: when Matariki rises before dawn in midwinter, the new year begins.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Krittika Round the World activity. You hear how different peoples tell stories about the same star cluster.

flow.do: Talk about what is the same and what is different.
flow.say: What is the same in these stories? Why do you think so many people saw women or sisters?
flow.kid: What is the same in the stories? Why do so many see sisters?

ask.q: Why might some stories have six women and some have seven?
good: Some people can see six stars and some can see seven.
One star is very faint.

flow.parent: Nobody knows for sure why the stories are so alike. Some astronomers think the story is very old and was carried round the world. Others think it was made up many times.

flow.do: Your child draws one story and makes up their own.
flow.say: Now you are a storyteller. Make up your own story about these stars. Who are they? Why are they so close together?
flow.kid: Make up your own story about these stars. Who are they? Draw it.
flow.think: Krittika's stars really were born together. Which story fits that best?

activities.title: Festival Stars: which festivals follow the nakshatras?

materials.item: a printed Tamil, Malayalam or other Indian calendar (panchangam), or the list in the note
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Find festivals named after a nakshatra, and the stars they belong to.

activities.record: Make a table: festival, nakshatra, and the star or stars it is named after.

flow.do: Show your child a printed calendar. Point to where it names the nakshatra for each day.
flow.say: This calendar tells us which nakshatra the Moon is in each day. Can you find today's?
flow.kid: Find today on the calendar. Which nakshatra is the Moon in today?
flow.parent: Many Tamil and Malayalam calendars print the nakshatra for each day, often in a corner of the date box. A sky app also shows which star group the Moon is in.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Festival Stars activity. You find out which festivals are timed by the Moon's nakshatra.

flow.do: Read out the festivals in the note. Your child fills in the table.
flow.say: Each of these festivals happens on the day the Moon is in a certain nakshatra. Let's make a table.
flow.kid: Listen to each festival. Write its name and its nakshatra in your table.
flow.parent: Onam: Thiruvonam, which is Shravana, in the month of Chingam. Karthigai Deepam: Krittika, in the month of Karthigai. Arudra Darshanam at Chidambaram: Thiruvathirai, which is Ardra, in Margazhi. Thaipusam: Pusam, which is Pushya, in the month of Thai. Panguni Uttiram: Uttiram, which is Uttara Phalguni, in Panguni.

flow.do: Ask the question below.
flow.say: The Moon visits all 27 nakshatras every month. So why is Onam only once a year?
flow.kid: The Moon visits Thiruvonam every month. So why is Onam once a year?

ask.q: Why is Onam only once a year?
good: Because it also has to be in the month of Chingam.
It needs the right nakshatra and the right month.

quiz.p: Most of the stars in a constellation are:
opts: at very different distances from us
touching each other
all the same distance from us
quiz.why: Constellations join stars that lie in the same direction from Earth. Their distances are usually very different. Picking 'all the same distance' is what the sky makes us think, because it looks like a flat dome.

quiz.p: In the Thread Saptarishi model, Meenakshi looked at the paper stars from the side. What did she see?
opts: A ladle, just like from the Earth card
Five paper stars close together, and two much further away
No paper stars at all
quiz.context: In the Thread Saptarishi experiment, seven threads run from a card with a hole (the Earth) to seven dots on a wall. A paper star sits on each thread at that star's real distance, 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years.
quiz.why: Five stars are about 80 light-years away and two are much further. From the side, the distance differences show. The ladle shows only from the Earth card.

quiz.p: In the thread model, why did the ladle show only from the hole in the Earth card?
opts: Because the paper stars are lined up along threads that all start there
Because the card is magic
Because the wall is flat
quiz.context: In the Thread Saptarishi experiment, seven threads run from a card with a hole (the Earth) to seven dots on a wall. A paper star sits on each thread at that star's real distance, 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years.
quiz.why: Each thread points from the Earth card to a star's direction. Only from the card do the paper stars sit in those directions. Real constellations work the same way, seen from Earth.

opts: The Moon takes about 27 days to go round the sky and come back to the same stars
There are 27 stars in the sky
The year has 27 weeks
quiz.why: One nakshatra for each day of the Moon's trip round the sky. The real time is about 27 and one-third days.

quiz.p: Tonight the Moon is in Rohini. About where will it be in two nights?
opts: Two nakshatras further east, in Ardra
Still in Rohini
On the other side of the sky
quiz.why: The Moon moves into about one new nakshatra each night. After Rohini comes Mrigashira, then Ardra.

quiz.p: The Greeks saw a hunter in the stars of Orion. Indian astronomers saw a deer's head there. What does this show?
opts: Different peoples join the same stars into different pictures
The Greeks and Indians saw different stars
One of them was wrong
quiz.why: The stars are the same for everyone. The pictures and stories come from the people. Neither is wrong.

quiz.p: In India, the Krittikas are six mothers. In Greece, the same stars are seven sisters. Why might the numbers differ?
opts: Most people see six stars there, and some see seven
The Greeks had better eyes
There are 13 stars in Krittika
quiz.why: In a tight cluster, some stars are near the limit of what eyes can see. Most people see six, and sharp eyes on a dark night see seven or more.

quiz.p: What did Edmond Halley find in 1718?
opts: Some bright stars had moved since Ptolemy's time
The Earth goes round the Sun
There are 88 constellations
quiz.why: Halley compared his star positions with Ptolemy's list from about 150 CE. Sirius and Arcturus were out of place. The 'fixed stars' were moving.

quiz.p: Why will the Saptarishi look different in about 50,000 years?
opts: Two of its stars move in different directions from the other five
The stars will burn out
The Earth will stop spinning
quiz.why: Five stars travel together. Kratu and Marichi move differently, so the ladle slowly bends.

quiz.p: Selvi, a girl in Madurai, goes onto the terrace to look for faint stars. What should she do first?
opts: Switch off nearby lights and wait about 20 minutes without looking at her phone
Look at her phone to find the stars quickly
Shine a bright white torch at the sky
quiz.why: Her eyes need 20 to 30 minutes of darkness to see faint stars. A bright phone screen or white torch undoes it. A dim red light is fine.

quiz.p: In the Eyes in the Dark test, why did you see more paper stars after 15 minutes than after 1 minute?
opts: My eyes got better at seeing in dim light
The stars on the paper got darker
The room got brighter
quiz.context: In the Eyes in the Dark experiment, you sit in a nearly dark room and count faint pencil stars on a paper after 1, 5, 10 and 15 minutes.
quiz.why: Nothing changed in the room. The cells in your eyes that work in dim light became more sensitive. This is dark adaptation.

quiz.p: Why do people in a big city see far fewer stars than people in a village?
opts: City lights light up the air, and faint stars are lost in the glow
There are fewer stars above cities
Tall buildings block all the stars
quiz.why: The stars are the same above every place. Light shining upwards in a city makes the sky glow, so only the brightest stars show through.

items.p: What is a constellation?
opts: A group of stars that are close together in space
A pattern of stars that people have named
A kind of planet
A very bright star
items.why: A constellation is a pattern people see and name, such as the Saptarishi or Orion. Its stars are usually far apart in space. Picking 'close together in space' is the most common mistake, and the thread model shows why it is wrong.

items.p: The seven stars of the Saptarishi are all the same distance from Earth.
items.why: False. Five are about 80 light-years away. Kratu is about 123 and Marichi about 104.

items.p: Indian astronomers split the Moon's path round the sky into ____ nakshatras.
items.why: The Moon takes about 27 and one-third days to go round the sky and come back to the same stars, so there is one nakshatra for each day.

items.p: Match each nakshatra to its star or star group.
pairs: the Pleiades, a tight star cluster
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each nakshatra is named after a star or star group that lies in that part of the Moon's path.

items.p: In the Thread Saptarishi model, where must your eye be to see the seven paper stars make a ladle?
opts: Anywhere in the room
At the hole in the Earth card
Right next to the wall
items.context: In the Thread Saptarishi experiment, seven threads run from a card with a hole (the Earth) to seven dots on a wall. A paper star sits on each thread at that star's real distance, 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years.
items.why: The paper stars line up into a ladle only when seen from the Earth card, because that is where all the threads start. One step to the side, and the shape bends. If you picked 'anywhere', try the model again from the side.

items.p: In the Thread Saptarishi model, the paper stars for Kratu and Marichi were much nearer the wall than the other five. What does that tell you about the real stars?
items.context: In the Thread Saptarishi experiment, seven threads run from a card with a hole (the Earth) to seven dots on a wall. A paper star sits on each thread at that star's real distance, 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years.
items.a: Kratu and Marichi are much further from Earth than the other five stars. They only seem to be part of one group because they lie in the same direction from Earth.
items.why: A strong answer links the model to the real sky: further along the thread means further from Earth, so the ladle is a pattern seen from here.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one help you see more stars, or hide stars?
items: looking at a bright phone screen
items.a: see items
items.why: Your eyes need time in the dark, and white light undoes it. Light in the sky, from streetlights or a full Moon, drowns out faint stars.

items.p: Why do stargazers cover their torches with red plastic?
opts: Red light looks like starlight
Red light disturbs the eyes' dark adaptation much less than white light
Red light is brighter
items.why: The cells that see in dim light are not very sensitive to red, so a dim red light lets you read a map without spoiling your night eyes. Red is not brighter, and starlight is many colours.

items.p: Put the steps of the Thread Saptarishi model in order.
items: Mark the seven star dots on paper on the wall
Tape the seven threads at the hole in the Earth card
Stretch each thread to its dot
Tape each paper star at its real distance
Look through the hole, then from the side
items.a: order shown
items.context: In the Thread Saptarishi experiment, seven threads run from a card with a hole (the Earth) to seven dots on a wall. A paper star sits on each thread at that star's real distance, 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years.
items.why: You need the dots before you can stretch the threads, and the threads before you can place the stars. You look last, from two places, to compare.

items.p: Draw the seven stars of the Saptarishi twice. First, as you see them from Earth. Second, as they would look from the side, at their real distances.
items.a: First drawing: a ladle, four stars in a bowl and three in a handle. Second drawing: five stars close together and two, Kratu and Marichi, much further away.
items.why: The two drawings show that a constellation's shape depends on where you look from.
items.art: Two empty boxes labelled 'from Earth' and 'from the side'.

items.p: The Moon moves into about one new nakshatra each day.
items.why: True. There are 27 nakshatras, and the Moon goes round the sky in about 27 days.

items.p: Karthigai Deepam is lit on the day the Moon is in which nakshatra?
opts: Krittika
Rohini
Thiruvonam
items.why: Karthigai Deepam is in the month of Karthigai, on Krittika day. The name Karthigai comes from Krittika. Thiruvonam is the nakshatra of Onam.

items.p: Meena, a girl in Class 3, says the Saptarishi is not real, because its stars are not together. Her grandmother says it is real, because everyone can see it. Their neighbour Asha, an astronomer, has a third view.

views.says: The stars are at different distances. The ladle is just an accident of where we are. It is not a real thing.
Everyone on Earth sees the same ladle, and people have seen it for thousands of years. That makes it real.
The stars are real, and the ladle is a real view from Earth. It just isn't a group of stars that belong together.

items.ask: Who do you agree with most? Give a reason from the thread model. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence: from the side, the paper stars did not make a ladle, so Meena has a point. But it also admits that from Earth the ladle really does show every time, as the grandmother says.
items.why: This is a real question about what 'real' means. Everyone agrees on the facts: the distances and the view from Earth. They disagree about whether a view counts as a real thing.

items.p: A ____ is the distance light travels in one year.
items.why: A light-year is about 9.5 lakh crore kilometres. It measures distance, not time.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Krittika
Rohini
Jupiter
Chitra
items.why: Krittika, Rohini and Chitra are nakshatras, named after stars. Jupiter is a planet. It wanders through the nakshatras over the years.

items.p: In the Eyes in the Dark test, you saw 3 stars after 1 minute and 10 stars after 15 minutes. Nothing on the paper changed. What changed, and how should that change the way you stargaze from your balcony?
items.context: In the Eyes in the Dark experiment, you sit in a nearly dark room and count faint pencil stars on a paper after 1, 5, 10 and 15 minutes.
items.a: My eyes changed. They became better at seeing in dim light the longer I stayed in the dark. So on the balcony I should switch off the lights, wait about 20 minutes, and not look at a phone.
items.why: A strong answer names dark adaptation as the cause, and uses it to plan a real night of stargazing.

items.p: In the Eyes in the Dark test, Divya's younger brother switches on the room light for a moment after 10 minutes. What will happen to her count?
opts: It goes up
It drops, and she has to wait again
It stays the same
items.context: In the Eyes in the Dark experiment, you sit in a nearly dark room and count faint pencil stars on a paper after 1, 5, 10 and 15 minutes.
items.why: Bright white light undoes much of the dark adaptation in a moment. Her eyes need several minutes in the dark again to recover.

items.p: Your fist held out at arm's length covers about ____ degrees of sky.
items.why: This is true for most children and grown-ups, because people with bigger hands also have longer arms.

items.p: In the Moon's Daily Step experiment, Kavya found the Moon was 1 fist east of a bright star on Monday and about 3 and a half fists east on Wednesday, at the same time. How far did the Moon move each night? About how long would it take to go all the way round the sky?
items.context: In the Moon's Daily Step experiment, you measure with your fist how far the Moon is from a bright star, at the same time on three nights.
items.a: About 1 and a quarter fists each night, because 2 and a half fists over 2 nights is about 1 and a quarter each. That is about 13 degrees a night. All the way round is 360 degrees, which takes about 27 nights.
items.why: A strong answer finds the change over two nights, halves it, and connects 27 nights to the 27 nakshatras.

items.p: In the Moon's Daily Step experiment, why must you look at the same time each night?
opts: Because the stars and the Moon move across the sky through the night as the Earth spins
Because the Moon only shines at 7:30
Because the star might switch off
items.context: In the Moon's Daily Step experiment, you measure with your fist how far the Moon is from a bright star, at the same time on three nights.
items.why: Everything in the sky moves from east to west through the night, because the Earth spins. Measuring at the same time keeps the test fair, so you only see the Moon's own movement among the stars.

items.p: Sort these into what is the same and what is different for a child in Kochi and a child in Delhi looking up on the same night.
items: the nakshatra the Moon is in
how high the Saptarishi is above the horizon
the names they may use for the stars
items.a: see items
items.why: The stars are so far away that both children see the same patterns and the Moon in the same nakshatra. Delhi is further north, so the northern stars sit higher in its sky. The languages and names they learnt may differ.

items.p: Edmond Halley compared his star positions with Ptolemy's old star list. What did he find?
opts: All the stars were exactly where Ptolemy put them
A few bright stars, such as Sirius and Arcturus, had moved
The stars had all moved together by the same amount
items.why: Most stars matched, but a few bright ones were out of place by about the width of the full Moon or more. Halley reasoned they had really moved. Picking 'exactly where Ptolemy put them' is the old idea of the fixed stars.

items.p: The stars of Krittika, the Pleiades, really are close together in space.
items.why: True. Krittika is a star cluster. Its stars were born together about 100 million years ago and are all about 440 light-years away. This is different from the Saptarishi.

items.p: Match each festival to its nakshatra.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these festivals falls on the day the Moon is in that nakshatra, in a particular month.

items.p: Draw the night sky above your balcony with three stars of different brightness. Draw the city lights below. Show with arrows how the city light hides the faintest star.
items.a: Arrows of light from streetlights going up and lighting the air. The faintest star is lost in that glow, while the brightest still shows.
items.why: Light pollution does not stop starlight. It adds a glow to the air, and the faint stars cannot be seen against it.
items.art: A blank sky above a row of buildings with streetlights.

items.p: Arcturus, the nakshatra Swati, has moved about twice the width of the full Moon since Ptolemy's time, nearly 1,900 years ago. Why does it still look fixed to us?
opts: It moves too slowly to see in one life, because it is so far away
It has stopped moving
Our eyes cannot see stars move
items.why: A star racing through space shifts only a tiny bit in our sky in a lifetime, because it is so far away. Over thousands of years the tiny shifts add up.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 4, says: 'The Moon is in Krittika tonight, so it will be in Krittika all month.' Use what you know about the nakshatras to explain his mistake.
items.a: The Moon moves east among the stars into about one new nakshatra each night. Tonight Krittika, tomorrow Rohini, the next night Mrigashira. It comes back to Krittika after about 27 nights.
items.why: A strong answer says how fast the Moon moves among the stars and gives the next nakshatras as evidence.

items.p: Many families in India know a child's birth nakshatra. Some say it is a lovely tradition. Some say it shapes a child's character. A scientist has tested that second idea.

views.says: We celebrate Priya's star birthday every year on Pooradam. It connects her to the sky and to our family.
A child's nakshatra decides what kind of person they will be.

views.who: A scientist who studies tests like Shawn Carlson's
views.says: When astrologers were tested carefully, they could not match people to their birth charts any better than guessing.

items.ask: Which views can be true at the same time? Give a reason. Then say what kind of claim each person is making: about family, about the stars, or about a test.
items.a: A strong answer sees that the grandmother and the scientist can both be right: celebrating a star birthday is a tradition and does not need the stars to shape anyone. Nandini makes a claim about the stars that careful tests have not supported.
items.why: Culture and science answer different questions. A tradition can be meaningful without being a claim about how the stars act on people.

items.p: Label the seven stars of the Saptarishi on the drawing with their Indian names: Kratu, Pulaha, Pulastya, Atri, Angiras, Vasishtha, Marichi. Then mark where Arundhati is.
items.a: Kratu at the top outer corner of the bowl, Pulaha below him, Pulastya at the bottom inner corner, Atri where the bowl meets the handle, then Angiras, Vasishtha and Marichi along the handle. Arundhati is a tiny star next to Vasishtha.
items.why: Kratu and Pulaha are the two 'pointer' stars of the bowl. Arundhati sits just beside Vasishtha, the middle star of the handle.
items.art: The seven stars of the Saptarishi as dots joined into a ladle, with seven blank label lines and one tiny unlabelled dot beside the middle star of the handle.

items.p: Which star pattern is the odd one out?
opts: The Saptarishi
Orion
Krittika
Scorpius
items.why: Krittika is a real star cluster: its stars were born together and travel together. The stars of the Saptarishi, Orion and Scorpius are mostly at very different distances.

items.p: Imagine you live on a planet round Kratu, the star at the corner of the Saptarishi's bowl. Would you see the Saptarishi? Explain using the thread model.
items.context: In the Thread Saptarishi experiment, seven threads run from a card with a hole (the Earth) to seven dots on a wall. A paper star sits on each thread at that star's real distance, 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years.
items.a: No. In the model, the ladle showed only from the Earth card. Kratu is about 43 light-years further away than the five middle stars, so from Kratu they would be in a completely different direction. You would not see a ladle. Kratu would be your own sun.
items.why: A strong answer uses the model's lesson, that the shape depends on where you look from, and reasons about the new viewpoint.

items.p: In about 50,000 years, the Saptarishi will look bent out of shape. Which stars will have moved away from the others?
opts: Kratu and Marichi, the two end stars
All seven, by the same amount
None, because stars are fixed
items.why: Five of the seven stars move through space together. Kratu and Marichi move in other directions, so over tens of thousands of years they drift out of the pattern.

items.p: The Thread Saptarishi model uses 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years. Krittika is about 440 light-years away. How long would its thread have to be? Would it fit in your room?
items.context: In the Thread Saptarishi experiment, seven threads run from a card with a hole (the Earth) to seven dots on a wall. A paper star sits on each thread at that star's real distance, 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years.
items.a: 440 divided by 2 is 220, so 220 centimetres, which is 2 metres and 20 centimetres. It might fit in a large room, but it would be much longer than the Saptarishi threads.
items.why: A strong answer does the division correctly and compares the result with the room and with the other threads.

items.p: Since 1922, astronomers everywhere use 88 official constellations, most of them with Greek and Latin names. India, China, the Maori and many other peoples have their own star patterns.

views.who: An astronomer at a world meeting
views.says: Everyone needs the same map, so that a star found in Chennai and a star found in Chile can be given the same address.
Our children should first learn Saptarishi, Krittika and the nakshatras. These names carry our history and festivals.
We can learn both, like knowing a place's Tamil name and its name on a map.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer takes a side with a reason, for example that a shared map is needed for science, and then admits that local names carry real history and help families find stars together.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. A single map lets astronomers work together. Local star patterns carry knowledge and culture that a single map leaves out.

items.p: Arundhati and Vasishtha are about 82 and 83 light-years away. Kratu and Pulaha are about 123 and 80. Which pair are true neighbours in space?
opts: Arundhati and Vasishtha
Kratu and Pulaha
Both pairs
items.why: Arundhati and Vasishtha differ by only about 1 light-year and move together. Kratu is about 43 light-years further away than Pulaha, so they only look close.

items.p: If a star looks faint, it must be further away than a bright star.
items.why: False. Some stars give out much more light than others. Kratu is the furthest of the Saptarishi stars, but he is one of its brightest. Brightness alone cannot tell you distance.

items.p: How could you test whether more stars are visible during a power cut than with the streetlights on? Plan a fair test.
items.a: Look at the same patch of sky from the same spot, at about the same time, after waiting 20 minutes in the dark both times. Count the stars inside a cardboard tube or a window frame. Do it once with the streetlights on and once in a power cut, on clear nights with no Moon.
items.why: A strong plan changes only the streetlights. It keeps the place, the patch of sky, the waiting time and the Moon the same.

items.p: Chinese and Arab astronomers had 28 stations for the Moon, while Indian astronomers mostly used 27. Why might they choose different numbers?
opts: The Moon takes about 27 and one-third days, so 27 or 28 are both close
The Moon moved faster in China
There are more stars in China
items.why: 27 and one-third is between 27 and 28, so either number is a fair choice. Some old Indian lists also had a 28th nakshatra, Abhijit.

items.p: Design a model, like the thread model, for Orion. Draw where you would place Betelgeuse (about 550 light-years away) and Bellatrix (about 250 light-years away) on their threads, using 1 centimetre for every 10 light-years.
items.a: Betelgeuse's paper star at about 55 centimetres along its thread, and Bellatrix's at about 25 centimetres.
items.why: 550 divided by 10 is 55, and 250 divided by 10 is 25. Betelgeuse is over twice as far away as Bellatrix, though both are 'shoulders' of Orion.
items.art: A blank card with a hole on the left and two lines to dots marked Betelgeuse and Bellatrix on the right.

items.p: Match each star pattern to a story told about it.
pairs: the fishhook of Maui (Hawaii and New Zealand)
a bear followed by hunters (the Mi'kmaq of Canada)
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each people joined the same stars into their own picture and story.

items.p: Sneha says: 'Halley must have been wrong. Ptolemy's list was just full of mistakes.' How did Halley answer that worry?
items.a: Halley noticed that most stars matched Ptolemy's list well. Only a few bright stars, like Sirius and Arcturus, were out of place by a lot. It is unlikely that Ptolemy would make large mistakes only on the brightest stars and not their neighbours. So those stars had really moved.
items.why: A strong answer explains that the pattern of the differences, not one difference, is the evidence.

items.p: Sort these into things science has measured and things that are cultural stories.
items: The Krittikas cared for baby Kartikeya
The Pleiades are about 100 million years old
Maui pulled up islands with his fishhook
The Moon goes round the sky in about 27 days
items.a: see items
items.why: Both kinds matter, but in different ways. Measurements can be checked by anyone with the right tools. Stories carry a people's memory and meaning.

items.p: From the Moon, would an astronaut see the Saptarishi in the same shape as we do?
opts: Yes, because the Moon is very close to Earth compared with the stars
No, it would be a completely different shape
No, because there are no stars in the Moon's sky
items.why: The Moon is about 1.3 light-seconds away, but the stars are tens of light-years away. Compared with that, the Moon is right next to Earth, so the patterns look the same. To change the shape, you must travel light-years.

items.p: On the drawing of the Moon's path, label: the Moon tonight, the Moon tomorrow, east, west, and one nakshatra.
items.a: The Moon tomorrow is about one nakshatra east of the Moon tonight. East is the direction the Moon moves among the stars.
items.why: The Moon moves east among the stars about 13 degrees each night, one nakshatra.
items.art: A curved band across the night sky with small star groups, two blank Moon circles and five blank label lines.

items.p: Lakshmi says the Saptarishi is 'real from here'. Write what you think she means, using the thread model and the story of Arundhati.
items.a: The ladle shape is real when you look from Earth, because the seven stars really do lie in those directions. But it is not a group of stars that belong together, because they are at different distances. Arundhati and Vasishtha are different: they really are close in space.
items.why: A strong answer separates the view from Earth and the real places in space, and uses the Arundhati pair as an example of true neighbours.

applications: Sailors and travellers have found their way at night by the stars for thousands of years, including sailors on the Indian Ocean.
Calendars: Indian calendars name the Moon's nakshatra for every day, and many festivals, from Onam to Karthigai Deepam, are timed by it.
Astronomers use the 88 constellations as addresses, so that anyone in the world can find the same star or comet.
Spacecraft find their direction with star trackers: small cameras that recognise star patterns, as a stargazer does.
The Gaia spacecraft measured the distances and movements of over a billion stars, showing how the constellations will change.
Birds such as indigo buntings, which fly at night, learn the stars round the Pole Star when young, and use them to keep their direction on their long journeys.
Planetariums, such as those in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Thiruvananthapuram, use star maps to show the sky as it was long ago or will be in the future.
Towns and parks that cut light pollution, called dark-sky places, let people see the stars again and protect night animals.

open_questions.q: Do Arundhati and Vasishtha go round each other?
open_questions.why_open: They are about the same distance away and move together. Astronomers are still working out whether gravity holds them together as a pair.

open_questions.q: How old are the oldest star stories?
open_questions.why_open: Some astronomers think the seven sisters story may be over 100,000 years old. Others think it was made up many times. There is no written record that old.

open_questions.q: How old is the list of nakshatras?
open_questions.why_open: The nakshatras appear in the Vedas, which are very old, but scholars disagree about exactly when those texts were composed.

open_questions.q: Do other animals see patterns in the stars?
open_questions.why_open: Some birds learn the turning of the stars round the Pole Star, and dung beetles use the Milky Way to roll in a straight line. Nobody knows what the night sky is like for them.

open_questions.q: How many of the stars we see have planets with life?
open_questions.why_open: Thousands of planets have been found round other stars, but no sign of life on any of them yet.
