maths.problem: In the Thread Saptarishi model, 1 centimetre stands for 2 light-years. Kratu is about 123 light-years away and Pulaha about 80. How far along their threads do their paper stars go? How much further from Earth is Kratu's paper star?
maths.answer: Kratu at about 62 centimetres, Pulaha at 40 centimetres. Kratu's paper star is about 22 centimetres further along.
maths.explain: 123 divided by 2 is 61 and a half, so about 62. 80 divided by 2 is 40. 62 minus 40 is 22.
maths.context: In the Thread Saptarishi experiment, seven threads run from a card with a hole (the Earth) to seven dots on a wall. A paper star sits on each thread at that star's real distance, 1 centimetre for every 2 light-years.
maths.why_maths: Real star distances are far too big for a room. Dividing by 2 turns light-years into centimetres, so the model shows the real pattern of near and far.

maths.problem: The Moon moves into about one new nakshatra each night. Tonight it is in Krittika, the 3rd nakshatra. Which number nakshatra will it be in after 7 nights? Use the list: 1 Ashwini, 2 Bharani, 3 Krittika, 4 Rohini, 5 Mrigashira, 6 Ardra, 7 Punarvasu, 8 Pushya, 9 Ashlesha, 10 Magha.
maths.explain: 3 plus 7 is 10. The 10th nakshatra in the list is Magha.
maths.context: This is about the nakshatras, the 27 star groups along the Moon's path. The Moon moves into about one new nakshatra each night.
maths.why_maths: Counting on along the list tells you where the Moon will be, without waiting for the nights to pass.

maths.problem: The Moon is in Revati, the 27th and last nakshatra. Where will it be in 3 nights? Remember that after the 27th comes the 1st again.
maths.explain: After Revati (27) comes Ashwini (1), then Bharani (2), then Krittika (3). So 3 nights after Revati, the Moon is in Krittika. Going round a circle, 27 plus 3 is 30, and 30 minus 27 is 3.
maths.context: This is about the nakshatras, which go round the sky in a circle of 27.
maths.why_maths: The nakshatras go round in a circle, like the hours on a clock, so after the last one you start again from 1.

maths.problem: In the Eyes in the Dark test, Lakshmi counted 3 stars after 1 minute, 6 after 5 minutes, 9 after 10 minutes and 10 after 15 minutes. Draw a bar chart. Between which two times did she gain the fewest stars? What does that tell you?
maths.answer: Between 10 and 15 minutes, when she gained only 1 star. Her eyes were getting close to their best.
maths.explain: From 1 to 5 minutes she gained 3. From 5 to 10 she gained 3. From 10 to 15 she gained only 1. The gains get smaller, because the eyes have nearly finished adapting.
maths.context: In the Eyes in the Dark experiment, you sit in a nearly dark room and count faint pencil stars on a paper after 1, 5, 10 and 15 minutes.

answer_chart.title: Stars Lakshmi saw in the dark (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance that the gains slow down, which tells you roughly how long to wait in the dark.

maths.problem: Light from Kratu takes about 123 years to reach us. If the light reaching your eye tonight left Kratu 123 years before 2026, in which year did it set off?
maths.explain: 2026 minus 123: 2026 minus 100 is 1926, and minus 23 more is 1903.
maths.context: This is about light-years. A star 123 light-years away sends light that takes 123 years to reach us.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting tells you how old the light is when it reaches you, so you can picture how long ago the star looked like that.

maths.problem: In the Moon's Daily Step experiment, the Moon moved about 13 degrees each night. A full circle round the sky is 360 degrees. About how many nights does the Moon take to go all the way round? Use 13 times 27 to check.
maths.explain: 13 times 27 is 351, which is very close to 360. 13 times 28 would be 364, a little too much. So about 27 nights, and a bit.
maths.context: In the Moon's Daily Step experiment, you measure with your fist how far the Moon is from a bright star, at the same time on three nights.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the Moon's step by the number of nights checks whether 27 nakshatras really fit one trip round the sky.

roots.context: We have been learning that a constellation is a pattern of stars seen from Earth, and that the Moon walks through the 27 nakshatras. Now we ask what star patterns tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the thread model, the seven paper stars made the Saptarishi only from the Earth card. From the side, two of them were far behind the other five. The real seven stars are spread out in space in the same way. So a constellation is a shape that the stars make only when seen from near Earth.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about a constellation as a group of stars, like a family living in one house. Most constellations are stars at very different distances, which only line up when seen from where we are.
deep_truth.evidence: In the thread model, the ladle showed only from the Earth card and broke apart from the side. Measured distances say the same: Kratu is about 123 light-years away and Pulaha, just below him, about 80.

three.who_am_i: You are standing in the one place where the Saptarishi is a ladle. Part of every star pattern you see comes from where you are.
three.what_is_life: Indigo buntings fly thousands of kilometres at night and need to keep their direction. As chicks they learn the stars that turn round the Pole Star, and use them to steer.
three.what_is_this_world: The stars are not stuck on a dome. They are scattered through deep space, near and far, and the flat sky is how that space looks from one small place.

roots.thread: There is one set of stars in space, and every people on Earth looks at it from the same place. Tamil families see Vasishtha and Arundhati. The Greeks saw a bear, and the Mi'kmaq of Canada see a bear followed by hunters. The stars are the same, and each people joined them into its own pictures and stories. In the same way, every place in space has its own sky made from the same stars. Each view is true from where it is seen, and none of them is the whole.

teachings.teaching: Truth is one, and the wise call it by many names.
teachings.link: The same seven stars are called the Saptarishi, the Plough, the Great Bear and a bear with hunters. There is one set of stars and many names and stories for it.

teachings.source: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, told in Jain teaching on anekantavada (many-sidedness) and in the Buddhist Udana 6.4
teachings.teaching: Each blind man touches one part of an elephant, a leg, the trunk or an ear, and is sure the elephant is like a pillar, a snake or a fan. Each is partly right, and none sees the whole animal.
teachings.link: From the Earth card the paper stars made a ladle. From the side they made a scattered group. Each view was true from its place, and you needed both to understand the stars.

science.text: The shape of a constellation depends on where you see it from. The Gaia spacecraft has measured the distances of over a billion stars, so astronomers can work out how our constellations would look from other stars.
Some astronomers think the seven sisters story told about Krittika in many cultures may be over 100,000 years old.

other_view.view: A constellation is a handy map region and a set of human stories. The stars themselves have nothing to do with our patterns. The meaning is in the people who tell the stories, not in the sky, and it is fine to enjoy them as stories.

practice.title: Two eyes, two views
practice.say: Let's sit quietly in a dim room. Hold up one finger at arm's length, in front of a far light or a picture on the wall. Close your left eye and look. Now open it and close your right eye. Did your finger jump? Each eye sees from a slightly different place, so each sees its own picture. Now close both eyes. Breathe slowly six times. When you open them, look round the room. Everything you see, you see from exactly here.
practice.kid: Hold up one finger. Close one eye. Now swap eyes. Did your finger jump? Each eye sees from its own place. Close your eyes. Breathe slowly six times. Open them and look round.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if in a city flat today, with the materials listed. The thread model was checked on paper: the seven dot positions make the ladle about 44 centimetres wide, which is the right size for the Saptarishi seen from 1 metre, so the paper stars sit on their dots when seen from the Earth card. The longest thread distance, Kratu at 62 centimetres, fits inside a 1 metre gap. The threads are taped at the edge of the hole rather than knotted through it, so the knot does not block the child's eye. The dark-room test uses pencil marks of different pressure and asks the parent to open or close the door if the child sees none or all at once. how_we_found_out.story: For about 2,000 years, astronomers called the stars the 'fixed stars'. The Moon, the Sun and the planets wandered across the sky, but the stars seemed to keep the same places against each other for ever. So the constellations would never change shape. In 1718, the English astronomer Edmond Halley tested this. He compared star positions measured in his own time with the star list in Ptolemy's book, the Almagest, made in Alexandria about 1,550 years earlier. Most stars matched. But a few bright stars, including Sirius and Arcturus, did not. They were out of place by about the width of the full Moon or more. Halley reasoned that Ptolemy could hardly have made such large mistakes on the brightest stars, while getting their neighbours right. So these stars must have moved. Later astronomers measured the movements of thousands of stars. Every star moves. They only look fixed because they are so far away. Arcturus is the nakshatra Swati, and it is one of the fastest-moving bright stars in our sky.
how_we_found_out.who: Edmond Halley, an English astronomer, using the star list of Ptolemy of Alexandria
how_we_found_out.when: 1718 (Ptolemy's star list is from about 150 CE)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the stars were fixed, so the constellations would keep the same shapes for ever. Halley showed that Sirius and Arcturus had moved since Ptolemy's time, so the stars do move and the patterns slowly change.
